(Com Reuters e Bloomberg)

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: FII TRXF11 conclui venda de 15 imóveis por R$ 207,25 milhões; veja lucro por cota
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: O conjunto negociado reúne 11 agências da Caixa Econômica Federal, duas lojas do GPA, um centro comercial e um imóvel ocupado por Americanas e Dasa
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O fundo imobiliário TRXF11 (TRX Real Estate) concluiu a venda de um portfólio com 15 imóveis por R$ 207,25 milhões ao BRC Renda Urbana FII.

A operação, anunciada inicialmente em junho, foi formalizada nesta segunda-feira (28), com a transferência dos empreendimentos para o comprador.

O conjunto negociado reúne 11 agências da Caixa Econômica Federal, duas lojas do GPA, um centro comercial e um imóvel ocupado por Americanas e Dasa.

Os ativos estão distribuídos por diferentes estados, incluindo São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Bahia, Paraná e Maranhão.

Venda deve gerar lucro de R$ 31,9 milhões

Segundo as estimativas divulgadas pelo TRXF11, a operação deve resultar em um ganho de capital de aproximadamente R$ 31,9 milhões, equivalente a cerca de R$ 0,51 por cota.

A transação também apresenta uma taxa interna de retorno (TIR) estimada em 38,49% ao ano. De acordo com o fundo, esse retorno corresponde a aproximadamente 107% do CDI durante o período em que os imóveis permaneceram na carteira.

A gestora TRX Investimentos afirmou que o preço negociado está alinhado aos valores indicados nos últimos laudos de avaliação dos imóveis.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Bets acionam STF, pedem relatoria de Fux e apontam 833 sites ilegais desde proibição
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Entidade pede que processo seja direcionado ao ministro, que já relata ações sobre o setor e associações reiteram pedido para suspender MP
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
Entidades que representam empresas de apostas entraram com uma nova ação no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) contra a medida provisória do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva que proibiu as bets no país e pediram que o processo fique sob a relatoria do ministro Luiz Fux. As associações também afirmam ter identificado 833 novos sites ilegais de apostas desde a entrada em vigor da proibição.

A Associação Nacional de Jogos e Loterias (ANJL) informou neste domingo a Fux que já protocolou uma ação direta de inconstitucionalidade contra a medida provisória. No mesmo processo, a entidade pede que o Supremo reconheça a constitucionalidade do marco legal que regulamentou as apostas no país.

A entidade pediu ainda que a nova ação seja distribuída a Fux por prevenção. O argumento é que o ministro já relata as três outras ações do mesmo tipo que discutem a constitucionalidade das regras do setor e têm objeto relacionado ao da nova ação. A prevenção é uma regra processual usada para concentrar em um mesmo relator processos que possuem conexão, evitando decisões conflitantes. A análise da prevenção, contudo, ainda será feita pela presidência do STF.

Segundo as entidades, a MP atingiu diretamente as normas que já são discutidas nas ações sob responsabilidade de Fux. Por isso, sustentam que ele deve também assumir a relatoria do novo processo. O pedido de prevenção ainda precisa ser analisado pelo Supremo.

Na manifestação encaminhada ao ministro, ANJL e Instituto Brasileiro de Jogo Responsável (IBJR) também reforçam o pedido para que os efeitos da MP sejam suspensos imediatamente. Como argumento de urgência, afirmam que houve um “exponencial e indevido aumento do mercado ilegal” desde a proibição.

Segundo a petição, um monitoramento do Observatório contra o Mercado Ilegal identificou 833 novos sites ilegais neste fim de semana. O número é apresentado pelas próprias entidades e não corresponde, na manifestação, a levantamento de um órgão público.

As associações alegam que, se a medida provisória continuar produzindo efeitos, o mercado regulado poderá ser desmontado antes mesmo de o Congresso concluir a análise da norma. Na avaliação delas, o crescimento das plataformas clandestinas também prejudicaria a proteção dos apostadores.

As entidades pedem a Fux que suspenda integralmente a MP até sua apreciação pelo Congresso ou até o julgamento da nova ação pelo STF, o que ocorrer primeiro. Nesse período, querem manter em vigor as autorizações concedidas às empresas, os atos regulamentares e a lista oficial de operadores autorizados.

Caso o ministro não suspenda toda a medida, as associações pedem, alternativamente, que seus efeitos sejam afastados para as empresas que já têm autorização para funcionar. Em última hipótese, querem um período de transição de pelo menos seis meses para o encerramento das operações.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Não há controle de preços de combustíveis e governo quer evitar alta, diz ministro
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Moretti também repetiu que há neutralidade fiscal nas medidas para conter altas de combustíveis
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti, avaliou nesta segunda-feira, 28, que o governo não busca “controlar” os preços de combustíveis no mercado brasileiro, mas evitar eventuais aumentos “abusivos”. A afirmação foi realizada durante coletiva de imprensa para tratar das últimas medidas tomadas para conter a alta dos preços diante da volatilidade dos preços internacionais do petróleo.

Moretti também repetiu que há neutralidade fiscal nas medidas para conter altas de combustíveis.

No fim da última semana, o governo federal prorrogou por 30 dias a subvenção ao óleo diesel em R$ 2,12 por litro. A subvenção econômica ao óleo diesel A, de uso rodoviário, estava prevista no âmbito das Medidas Provisórias (MP) 1.363 e 1.391.

A coletiva desta segunda-feira também trata da chamada “Operação Carga Pesada”, voltada à fiscalização do mercado de combustíveis e à apuração de possíveis aumentos “abusivos” nas margens de lucro do setor.

O ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Wellington Lima e Silva, relatou caso com alta de 1.300% na margem de lucro no setor de combustíveis.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Lula resiste a ir a debate da Globo e quer adiar confronto com Flávio para 2º turno
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Candidato do PL confirmou que vai participar de encontro independetemente da presença de petista
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato do PT à reeleição, indicou a aliados resistência em participar do debate da TV Globo, na quinta-feira. Um dos argumentos citados no entorno presidencial para a possível ausência é o receio do petista em se tornar alvo principal dos demais adversários.

A participação no encontro foi discutido com aliados na manhã desta segunda-feira, antes de Lula embarcar para compromissos em Belém (PA). Participaram da reunião integrantes do núcleo duro da campanha, como o presidente do PT, Edinho Silva, o ministro da Secretaria de Comunicação Social do governo, Sidônio Palmeira, o marqueteiro da campanha, Raul Rabelo, além de Paulo Okamoto, um dos principais conselheiros do petista.

Pessoas próximas a Lula afirmam que martelo não foi batido, mas a tendência é que o petista não compareça ao confronto. A agenda de campanha do PT para quinta-feira, data do debate na TV, segue em aberta.

Aliados se dividem sobre a presença de Lula no debate da TV Globo, realizado a três dias do primeiro turno. O grupo que defende a participação do petista afirma que o programa é a única oportunidade de ele confrontar Flavio Bolsonaro (PL) diretamente em rede nacional e horário de ampla audiência antes da votação. Também veem a chance de expor fragilidade do presidenciável do PL na disputa pelo voto de indecisos.

Os que defendem declinar do convite reclamam do formato do embate e temem que o confronto direto entre Lula e Flavio fique comprometido pela participação dos demais presidenciáveis nas perguntas e respostas. O presidente do PT e coordenador da campanha, Edinho Silva, afirmou nesta segunda-feira que a Lula não deverá ir ao debate.

— Lula quer ir ao debate desde que ele possa confrontar o que ele pensa, o que ele defende, o modelo que ele defende para o Brasil com o que Flavio Bolsonaro representa, ele fazer uma pergunta e ficar 20 minutos esperando todo mundo falar, se for esse modelo, evidente, ele não irá ao debate e ficará aguardando o segundo turno em que será só ele e o Flavio — disse a Rádio TMC.

A legislação eleitoral prevê que emissoras de rádio e televisão devem convidar candidatos de partidos, federações ou coligações que tenham, no mínimo, cinco parlamentares no Congresso Nacional.

Enquanto Lula resiste a participar do debate da TV Globo, a campanha de Flávio mudou o cálculo e decidiu que o candidato irá ao encontro. A reavaliação ocorreu em meio ao acirramento da disputa presidencial e após o episódio envolvendo Nossa Senhora Aparecida, que gerou desgaste para a campanha. A história foi impulsionada nas redes sociais após um debate sobre um projeto de lei arquivado há quase 20 anos que tinha o objetivo de retirar o título de padroeira do Brasil.

Até a semana passada, a orientação era outra. Flávio condicionava sua presença à participação de Lula, e integrantes da campanha avaliavam que havia pouco a ganhar em um debate sem o presidente. Nesse cenário, o candidato do PL poderia se tornar o principal alvo dos demais adversários enquanto o petista ficaria fora do confronto

No domingo, contudo, Flávio afirmou que participará do debate mesmo que Lula não compareça.

— Ele (Lula) que lute. Eu quero ir para lá para debater com ele. Então, estou chamando o Lula para o debate. Lula, eu quero você no debate da Globo. Vem debater comigo, porque eu vou esfregar a verdade na sua cara e vou mostrar ao brasileiro — afirmou.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Novo Desenrola⁠: Caixa e BB devem fazer cobranças dos devedores em novo programa
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Lançado às vésperas das eleições, medida prevê compra pelo governo de carteiras de débitos de até R$ 10 mil
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva prevê que a Caixa Econômica Federal e o Banco do Brasil (BB) devem ficar responsáveis pela cobrança dos beneficiados pelo Desenrola 3.0, de acordo com o desenho inicial da nova versão do programa para aliviar o orçamento das famílias endividadas.

A definição do formato final da operacionalização do programa ainda dependerá, no entanto, de reuniões técnicas entre o governo, os bancos e os demais credores.

No Desenrola 3.0, o governo vai comprar as carteiras de dívidas bancárias e não bancárias de até R$ 10 mil, inadimplidas entre 2 anos e 4 anos e meio. Serão selecionadas as carteiras dos credores que oferecerem o maior desconto ao governo.

O formato difere das versões anteriores do Desenrola Brasil, em que a participação do governo se restringia a garantir, por meio de um fundo público, as renegociações das dívidas.

O objetivo é acabar com até R$ 150 bilhões em dívidas das famílias brasileiras. A proposta é que a União compre com desconto mínimo de 90% as dívidas das instituições financeiras credoras e repasse esse desconto para os devedores, que poderão quitar a dívida à vista ou parcelar o saldo remanescente.

A operacionalização do programa ainda está sendo alinhada pelo governo com todos as partes interessadas. Nas conversas com o setor privado, a prioridade neste momento é preparar o leilão com os credores.

É necessário, por exemplo, fechar o formato do leilão, montar regras de verificação e a auditoria das carteiras. Depois de lançar o edital do leilão, a expectativa é de que demore cerca de três meses para leiloar, homologar o resultado, assinar o contrato com os credores e receber as carteiras.

De acordo com interlocutores a par do assunto, a ideia inicial é constituir um fundo de investimento em direitos creditórios (FIDC), em que o Tesouro Nacional seria o único cotista, para comprar as carteiras de dívidas. Depois da aquisição, a Caixa e o BB ficariam responsáveis pela cobrança às pessoas beneficiadas, considerando a expertise das instituições financeiras nesse tipo de gestão.

Desta vez, a participação dos devedores não deve depender de adesão ou anuência prévia. Caso a pessoa tenha um débito na carteira comprada pelo governo, automaticamente está no programa. Os descontos obtidos pela União junto aos credores serão repassados aos devedores, que, por sua vez, poderão quitar a dívida à vista ou parcelar o saldo remanescente, acrescido de juros.

Pelo lado privado, ainda são dúvidas se haverá uma plataforma para o leilão e como serão definidos os lotes. Pelo cronograma divulgado pelo governo, é esperada a publicação do chamamento para entrega de propostas para o leilão em novembro e a entrega das propostas em dezembro.

As propostas selecionadas devem ser homologadas em janeiro. Já em fevereiro, deve acontecer a assinatura dos contratos com os credores e o início do repasse do deságio aos devedores (quitação à vista ou parcelamento).

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Câncer em gatos revela pistas para tratamentos em humanos; entenda
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Estudo mapeou tumores em gatos e encontrou semelhanças genéticas que podem ajudar na busca por novos tratamentos contra o câncer.
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
Gatos domésticos podem se tornar aliados na busca por novos tratamentos contra o câncer em humanos. Um estudo internacional identificou semelhanças genéticas entre tumores que surgem naturalmente nos felinos e diferentes tipos da doença encontrados em pessoas. 

Publicado na revista Science, o trabalho analisou o DNA de 493 amostras e criou o primeiro grande mapa genético do câncer em gatos. Entre os achados, estão alterações em genes associados ao desenvolvimento de tumores que também aparecem com frequência em pacientes humanos.

Um dos exemplos é o TP53, que apresentou mutações em 33% das amostras analisadas. Em um levantamento anterior com cânceres humanos, a alteração estava presente em 34% dos casos.

As semelhanças não param na genética. Como convivem no mesmo ambiente que seus tutores, os gatos também ficam expostos a condições semelhantes às dos seres humanos, diferentemente de animais criados especificamente para pesquisas em laboratório.

“Eles também sofrem de muitas das mesmas doenças que os humanos, apoiando a ideia de que essas duas espécies compartilham pelo menos alguns mecanismos básicos de doença”, afirmou Bruce Kornreich, diretor do Cornell Feline Health Center.

  • Leia também: Anvisa investiga casos de cegueira súbita associados a canetas emagrecedoras

Câncer de mama revelou uma das principais semelhanças

Um dos achados mais relevantes apareceu nos carcinomas mamários felinos, tumores conhecidos pela alta agressividade.

A equipe identificou sete genes capazes de contribuir para o desenvolvimento da doença quando sofrem determinadas mutações. Entre eles está o FBXW7, alterado em mais da metade dos tumores mamários felinos estudados.

O mesmo gene também tem importância no câncer de mama humano. Em pacientes, mutações no FBXW7 costumam estar associadas a prognósticos piores.

A análise foi além da comparação genética. Em culturas de tecidos em laboratório, alguns tratamentos de quimioterapia tiveram maior eficácia contra tumores felinos com essas mutações.

O resultado ainda precisa ser confirmado em estudos mais amplos e não significa que já exista um novo tratamento contra o câncer em humanos. Mas abre caminho para investigar terapias que possam funcionar em tumores com características genéticas semelhantes nas duas espécies.

O estudo também encontrou paralelos em cânceres do sangue, ossos, pulmões, pele, trato gastrointestinal e sistema nervoso central.

Por que estudar o câncer em gatos pode ajudar humanos?

Uma das vantagens é que esses animais desenvolvem câncer naturalmente e vivem em ambientes semelhantes aos nossos.

No carcinoma de células escamosas da pele, por exemplo, foram identificados tumores felinos associados à radiação ultravioleta. O mesmo tipo de exposição está ligado a diferentes cânceres de pele em humanos.

Essa abordagem se aproxima do conceito de One Health, que integra a saúde humana e animal. Dados da medicina veterinária podem abrir novas linhas de investigação em pessoas, enquanto avanços da oncologia humana também podem beneficiar os gatos.

Os dados das 493 amostras foram reunidos em um recurso aberto à comunidade científica. A partir dele, outros grupos poderão investigar com mais profundidade como os tumores se desenvolvem e como diferentes espécies respondem aos mesmos medicamentos.

“Agora podemos começar a dar os próximos passos rumo à oncologia felina de precisão”, afirmou Louise Van Der Weyden, do Wellcome Sanger Institute e autora sênior do estudo.

O trabalho reuniu pesquisadores do Wellcome Sanger Institute, no Reino Unido, da Cornell University, da Universidade de Guelph, no Canadá, e da Universidade de Berna, na Suíça.

medium.titulo: Why AI Sales Agents Need Memory: What We Learned While Building DealMind
medium.resumo: AI assistants can answer questions quickly, but answering a question is only one part of helping with a long-running sales process.
medium.conteudo_html:
AI assistants can answer questions quickly, but answering a question is only one part of helping with a long-running sales process.

Sales conversations happen across multiple meetings. A customer may explain their requirements in one meeting, discuss pricing in another, raise technical concerns later, and then request a product demonstration.

If an AI assistant treats every interaction as a completely new conversation, important context can easily be lost.

While working on our HackWithHyderabad hackathon project, our team explored this problem by building DealMind, an AI-powered deal intelligence agent with persistent memory.

The problem with conversations without memory

Imagine that a salesperson has several conversations with the same customer.

During the first conversation, the customer explains what they are looking for.

In another conversation, they mention that they are also evaluating Salesforce.

Later, the customer raises concerns about pricing and asks for flexible pricing.

During another discussion, the technical team raises concerns about integration effort and implementation risk.

There may also be a security review required before the contract can be signed.

All of these details are important.

The challenge is bringing them together when preparing for the next meeting.

This is the problem we wanted DealMind to explore.

What we wanted DealMind to do

Our goal was to create an AI agent that could maintain context about a deal instead of starting from zero every time.

The idea was straightforward:

Store important interactions → retrieve relevant information → use that context to prepare useful meeting intelligence.

This became the foundation of our project.

Instead of treating every meeting as an isolated conversation, DealMind keeps relevant deal information available for future interactions.

Hindsight as the memory layer

For the persistent memory component, we used Hindsight.

The main workflow we explored was:

Retain → Recall → Reflect

Each step has a different purpose.

Retain

When a customer interaction takes place, relevant information can be retained as memory.

For example, details about customer requirements, pricing concerns, competitors, decision makers, technical concerns, and follow-up requests can become part of the stored deal context.

The important part is that this information does not have to disappear when the current conversation ends.

Recall

When information about a particular deal is needed later, relevant memories can be retrieved.

This allows the agent to use information from previous interactions instead of relying only on the current conversation.

For a salesperson preparing for a meeting, this can bring earlier customer information back into the conversation.

Reflect

The accumulated context can then be used to generate useful meeting intelligence.

This is where the stored information becomes useful for preparing for a future interaction.

Instead of simply showing a collection of old messages, the system can use the available context to produce a more organized view of the deal.

A simple example with ACME Corp

We used an example deal involving ACME Corp to demonstrate the workflow.

ACME was interested in an enterprise analytics platform to improve sales performance visibility and reporting.

At the same time, the customer was evaluating Salesforce as an alternative solution.

The CTO was the final technical decision maker.

The customer also felt that the current pricing was too high and requested a revised proposal with flexible pricing.

There were technical concerns around integration effort and implementation risk.

A security review was also required before the contract could be signed.

The sales operations team requested a live product demonstration.

Each of these details came from different parts of the deal context.

When they are considered together, they provide a much clearer picture of what needs attention before the next customer interaction.

Why context matters before a meeting

Suppose a salesperson is preparing for the next conversation with ACME.

Looking only at the most recent message may not provide enough information.

The salesperson may also need to remember:

  • What the customer is trying to achieve
  • Which alternative solution they are evaluating
  • Who is involved in the decision
  • What pricing concerns have been raised
  • What technical concerns exist
  • Which actions are still pending
  • What information is still unknown

This is the type of context DealMind is designed to bring together.

Instead of manually searching through previous conversations, the salesperson can use the available deal context to prepare for the next discussion.

From stored information to useful intelligence

One of the things we learned while working on DealMind is that memory by itself is not the final goal.

Simply storing information does not automatically make an AI agent useful.

The important part is being able to use the stored information when it is relevant.

For example, knowing that a customer requires a security review becomes much more useful when that information is visible while preparing for a future meeting.

Similarly, knowing that a customer has pricing concerns can keep that issue visible when planning the next steps.

The value comes from connecting information across time.

The architecture behind our idea

We kept the application architecture relatively simple.

The frontend provides the interface through which the salesperson interacts with DealMind.

The FastAPI backend handles the application logic and communication with the memory layer.

Hindsight provides the persistent memory capability.

The overall flow can be represented as:

Salesperson → DealMind Frontend → FastAPI Backend → Hindsight → Meeting Intelligence

This structure allowed us to focus on the main problem: how an AI agent can maintain useful context across customer interactions.

What we learned about AI agents

Building DealMind changed the way we thought about AI agents.

It is easy to think of an AI assistant as a system that receives a prompt and produces a response.

But many real-world tasks are not single conversations.

They are ongoing processes.

Sales is one example.

A customer relationship can continue across meetings, demonstrations, technical discussions, pricing conversations, and follow-ups.

For these workflows, access to relevant previous information can be an important part of the experience.

Memory is useful when it has a purpose

Another lesson from the project was that the goal is not simply to collect as much information as possible.

The goal is to make relevant information available when it is needed.

For DealMind, useful context includes customer requirements, concerns, decision makers, competitors, pending actions, and other deal-related information.

That context can then support meeting preparation.

In other words, we were not trying to build a system that simply remembers everything.

We wanted to explore a system where memory contributes to a specific workflow.

Building DealMind during a hackathon

Working on DealMind as a hackathon project gave our team the opportunity to connect several technologies into one practical application.

Our project involved frontend development, a FastAPI backend, Hindsight for persistent memory, and the application logic needed to turn stored deal information into meeting intelligence.

The most interesting part was not any single technology.

It was understanding how these pieces could work together around a real-world problem.

We also had to think about what information should be retained, how it should be associated with a deal, and how the accumulated context could be used later.

What we would like to explore further

There are several directions we could explore beyond the current version.

For example, a future version could make it easier to track changes in a deal over time, surface unresolved questions, and connect upcoming actions with previously recorded customer interactions.

There is also room to make the meeting preparation experience more interactive, so that a salesperson can ask follow-up questions about a deal instead of receiving only one generated brief.

These are areas we would like to explore as we continue developing the idea.

Final thoughts

Our experience with DealMind showed us that the usefulness of an AI agent can depend heavily on the context available to it.

A conversation that happened yesterday can matter during today’s meeting.

A concern raised earlier can become an important part of the next step in a deal.

Persistent memory gives an AI agent a way to maintain that context across interactions.

For our team, the main takeaway from building DealMind was simple:

An AI agent can be more useful when it doesn’t have to forget everything between conversations.

Building DealMind was a valuable experience for our team because it allowed us to move beyond simply generating AI responses and think about how an agent can work with information over time.

That is the idea we wanted to explore with DealMind.

medium.titulo: Why My Agent’s Hindsight Memory Isn’t a Chat Log
medium.resumo: What TOM retains, what it recalls, and how one stored correction turns into a different file plan
medium.conteudo_html:
What TOM retains, what it recalls, and how one stored correction turns into a different file plan

My agent filed my electricity bill and my AWS invoice in Documents/, next to a resume and a text file of project notes. No amount of chat history was going to fix that, because the mistake wasn’t a lack of context. It was a default that didn’t match how I work.

That is the difference I care about between a transcript and memory. A transcript records what was said. Memory has to be retrievable later, for a specific task, in a form the agent can act on. I built that layer in TOM, a local Python desktop agent, on top of Hindsight agent memory.

Where Hindsight sits

TOM has a Tkinter desktop app, a CLI and voice input, and all of them hand task requests to one TomAgent. Hindsight is reached through a single wrapper, tools/hindsight_memory.py. It builds a hindsight_client.Hindsight client lazily, so the agent still starts if the package or the key is missing.

You can point it at Hindsight Cloud with an API key, or at a self-hosted server with HINDSIGHT_BASE_URL. The bank ID is stable per install: HINDSIGHT_BANK_ID if set, otherwise a random tom-… ID saved under tom_brain/hindsight/. On first use the wrapper creates the bank with a short mission that tells Hindsight what to learn about this user and to prefer the most recent instruction when two conflict. That last clause matters. If I say PDFs go to Invoices today and Bills next month, I want the newer one to win.

The Hindsight documentation covers the client calls; the wrapper adds a 12 second timeout, two attempts, and a local journal.

What I retain

I retain two kinds of records, and they are tagged differently so recall can filter them.

Preferences and corrections. When I say “No, PDFs always go in Invoices, not Documents,” _retain_preference() stores the correction together with the request it corrects and TOM’s previous reply. It tags the record preference, a category such as file_organization, and correction when it is one. My exact words go into metadata.

# simplified from agent.py

tags = [TAG_PREFERENCE, category] + ([TAG_CORRECTION] if correction else [])

self.memory.retain(content, tags=tags, index_now=True,

metadata={“user_words”: command[:400], “category”: category})

index_now=True asks Hindsight to finish extracting facts before the call returns, so a correction is recallable on the very next request.

Task outcomes. After a task, _retain_outcome() stores what I asked, how TOM handled it, the status, and any rules it applied, tagged task. Those are cheap to write and give the bank a history of what worked.

What I recall

There are two recall paths. For ordinary requests, execute_task() starts a general recall as a background task while the NLP parser runs, so it adds no serial step. Handlers that draft emails or documents fold the hits into their prompts through _build_memory_context(). Voice mode does the same with a smaller limit.

File organization gets its own path, remembered_folder_rules(). It asks a file-specific question, filters to preference and correction tags, and returns up to 12 hits. If Hindsight returns facts but the text parser finds no rule, it falls back to reflect() with a JSON schema and asks for structured rules.

reflect() also powers a plain question: “what have you learned about me?” returns a grouped summary of what is in the bank.

Making memory inspectable

Retaining facts you can’t look at is uncomfortable. TOM has a Memory view with a Recall box and a “What have you learned?” button. Recall shows the stored facts behind a behavior, and “Recently stored” lists the latest items from the local journal.

Retained content is capped at 4,000 characters, and context and metadata values at 200 each, so a runaway reply can’t bloat the bank.

Before and after

Same folder, same agent, one correction in between.

After the correction, I added new files and reworded the request. TOM recalled the rule, showed it in a “Remembering” card, and asked for approval before moving anything.

The plan is built by ordinary Python. Hindsight decides what I prefer; the code decides where each file goes.

What I would tell you before you copy this

• Store tagged facts, not transcripts. A small, stable tag set (preference, correction, task) is what makes filtered recall possible.

• Write the correction with its context. “Not Documents” means nothing without the reply it corrects.

• Turn recalled text into a constrained object. Mine becomes a FolderRule before it can touch a file.

• Don’t treat the local journal as proof of storage. It mirrors what I retained. It does not confirm Hindsight accepted it.

• Know the limits. Only handlers that call recall benefit from memory, and rules match by extension, so a PDF that isn’t an invoice still follows the PDF rule.

I don’t fine-tune anything. The model is unchanged; the behavior changes because the right fact comes back at the right time. If you want the background, Vectorize has a good explanation of what agent memory is, and the code is in the TOM repository.

medium.titulo: Why I Put a Human Between My Incident Agent and Production
medium.resumo: Why I Put a Human Between My Incident Agent and Production
medium.conteudo_html:
Why I Put a Human Between My Incident Agent and Production

An incident-response agent can find a plausible fix in seconds.

That doesn’t mean I want it executing that fix in production in seconds.

When I built our incident-response workflow, I focused on a different problem: how do we let an agent investigate, learn from previous incidents, and recommend an action without turning a probabilistic decision into an uncontrolled production change?

The answer became a deliberately structured loop:

Recall → Reflect → Recommend → Approve → Remediate → Verify → Retain

Hindsight provides the memory layer, but the interesting engineering work is what happens around it.

Start with evidence, not action

Our active incident is INC-1057, affecting the Payment API.

The system reports:

Service:        Payment API
Severity:       SEV-1
HTTP 503:       38%
Database usage: 100%
DB pool:        50 → 10
Deployment:     payment-api-v3.1.0

A naive incident agent could immediately generate something like:

“The database is overloaded. Restart the application.”

That is exactly the behavior I wanted to avoid.

The system first investigates the incident against historical experience stored in Hindsight.

The investigation query asks for similar incidents and their outcomes.

investigation_query = f"""
Investigate this production incident:
Service: {incident["service"]}
Severity: {incident["severity"]}
HTTP error rate: {incident["error_rate"]}
Database usage: {incident["database_usage"]}
Recent deployment: {incident["deployment"]}
Database pool change: {incident["pool_change"]}
Find similar historical incidents and their outcomes.
"""

The agent therefore starts with evidence rather than an immediate action.

Recall and Reflect have different jobs

I deliberately separated Recall and Reflect.

Recall retrieves relevant experiences:

recall_result = client.recall(
    bank_id=BANK_ID,
    query=investigation_query
)

Reflect then reasons over the incident and historical experience:

reflection = client.reflect(
    bank_id=BANK_ID,
    query=analysis_query
)

That separation makes the workflow easier to reason about.

Recall asks:

What has happened before?

Reflect asks:

What does that experience tell us about this incident?

The historical incidents repeatedly connect deployment-related connection-pool configuration changes with database connection exhaustion.

They also contain a useful counterexample: an application restart that failed to resolve a similar incident.

The resulting recommendation is:

DB-CONNECTION-POOL-ROLLBACK

But a recommendation isn’t an authorization.

The recommendation stops at the safety boundary

The next stage is human approval.

The workflow explicitly asks:

approval = input(
    "\nApprove the simulated remediation? (yes/no): "
).strip().lower()
if approval not in ["yes", "y"]:
    print("\nHuman approval not granted.")
    print("Incident workflow stopped safely.")
    raise SystemExit

That small boundary changes the architecture considerably.

The agent is responsible for:

Investigation
Reasoning
Evidence
Recommendation

The operator remains responsible for:

Authorization

And the remediation layer is responsible for:

Execution
Verification

Those responsibilities don’t have to belong to the same component.

The current executor is intentionally simulated

The remediation stage in the current implementation is explicit about what it is doing:

[SIMULATION]
→ Stop affected deployment
→ Restore previous database pool configuration
→ Restore pool size: 50
→ Restart affected service

No real production action is performed.

I think this is an important limitation to be honest about.

The architecture demonstrates the complete decision loop, but the current executor is a simulated production environment rather than a live infrastructure control plane.

That is preferable to pretending that a prototype remediation command is production-safe.

The interesting part is that the interface between reasoning and execution is already explicit.

A future production implementation could connect that boundary to controlled infrastructure automation with appropriate authorization, audit, rollback, and policy checks.

Verification is a separate stage

After remediation, the workflow doesn’t simply declare success.

It checks concrete recovery signals:

verification = {
    "Database connection usage": "100% → 42%",
    "HTTP 503 error rate": "38% → 0.4%",
    "Service health": "DEGRADED → HEALTHY",
    "Deployment configuration": "Restored"
}

The resulting state is:

Database usage       100% → 42%
HTTP 503 errors       38% → 0.4%
Service             DEGRADED → HEALTHY

This distinction matters because an action can complete successfully while the incident remains unresolved.

For example:

Command executed successfully
            ≠
Service recovered successfully

The verification stage exists to measure the second condition.

Then comes the part most incident tools stop at

Once recovery is verified, the workflow generates a postmortem.

But instead of treating the postmortem as the end of the process, the system retains it in Hindsight.

client.retain(
    bank_id=BANK_ID,
    content=f"""
Completed Production Incident
{postmortem}
Outcome:
Successful recovery.
Historical Learning:
The DB-CONNECTION-POOL-ROLLBACK runbook successfully restored
service after database connection pool misconfiguration.
"""
)

Now the incident has become organizational memory.

That creates a loop:

┌───────────────────────┐
             │     New Incident      │
             └───────────┬───────────┘
                         ↓
                    HINDSIGHT
                     RECALL
                         ↓
                     REFLECT
                         ↓
                   RECOMMEND
                         ↓
                 HUMAN APPROVAL
                         ↓
                    REMEDIATE
                         ↓
                     VERIFY
                         ↓
                    POSTMORTEM
                         ↓
                    HINDSIGHT
                     RETAIN
                         │
                         └──────────────→ Future Incident

This is why I think of the system as a learning loop rather than just an incident chatbot.

A useful failure is part of the memory

One of the historical incidents in the system used:

APPLICATION-RESTART

The outcome was:

Failed

That failure is intentionally preserved.

If the agent only remembered successful actions, it could repeatedly recommend the same plausible but ineffective remediation.

With both positive and negative experiences available, the agent can distinguish:

What worked

from:

What was tried and failed

That is a much more realistic model of operational knowledge.

Engineers don’t just remember successful commands.

We remember the commands that wasted twenty minutes too.

The before-and-after behavior

The clearest difference is the workflow itself.

Without memory

Alert
 ↓
Analyze current metrics
 ↓
Generate likely fix
 ↓
Execute

With memory

Alert
 ↓
Recall similar incidents
 ↓
Compare outcomes
 ↓
Reflect on evidence
 ↓
Recommend remediation
 ↓
Human approval
 ↓
Execute
 ↓
Verify recovery
 ↓
Retain the lesson

The second workflow has two properties I care about.

First, the recommendation has historical context.

Second, the resolution becomes future context.

That’s the part that makes Hindsight more than a retrieval dependency in this architecture.

What I learned building the workflow

1. Don’t confuse autonomy with removing every human decision

For production systems, I would rather have an agent produce a strong, evidence-backed recommendation than silently execute an uncertain one.

The human approval stage is therefore part of the design, not an afterthought.

2. Separate recommendation from execution

The recommendation:

DB-CONNECTION-POOL-ROLLBACK

is data.

Executing that runbook is an operational action.

Keeping those stages separate makes the system easier to secure and evolve.

3. Verification should produce the next memory

A successful command isn’t enough.

The system needs to know whether the service actually recovered before it records the experience as successful learning.

4. Negative knowledge is valuable

The failed application restart is useful precisely because it failed.

Future incident reasoning should have access to unsuccessful experiments as well as successful remediations.

5. Memory creates a feedback loop

The biggest conceptual shift was realizing that the postmortem isn’t the final artifact.

It can become input to the next incident.

The lifecycle becomes:

Respond
→ Verify
→ Remember
→ Respond better

That’s the idea I wanted to explore with Hindsight’s documentation: memory shouldn’t just make an agent’s prompt longer. It should change how the system behaves over time.

The current implementation is deliberately cautious: the remediation is simulated and the operator approves it.

But the architecture points toward something more interesting than a chatbot.

It points toward an incident-response system that can accumulate operational experience without giving up the safety boundaries that production systems require.

And that, to me, is the useful version of an autonomous agent: not one that acts without humans, but one that makes the human decision better informed by everything the system has already learned.

medium.titulo: Starting Over at 34: From Administration to My First UX Internship
medium.resumo: How going back to school led me from UX student to product thinker, prompt engineer and AI design orchestrator at a startup.
medium.conteudo_html:
How going back to school led me from UX student to product thinker, prompt engineer and AI design orchestrator at a startup.

Last year, at 34, I made a decision that felt both exciting and terrifying:

I quit my largely manual administrative job and started over with a completely new career: I enrolled in a two-year programme in UX design.

This was not a small change. I was leaving behind a career I understood and entering a field where almost everything was new to me. I had never worked as a designer, and before starting my studies, I had barely used AI at all.

The first year of the programme was about building a foundation.

We learned the principles of user-centred design, design thinking, usability heuristics, accessibility and agile methods and we applied these principles in school projects.

The year went by quickly.

Then, in our second year, we started our first eight-week internship.

I thought this would be the moment when I could finally apply everything I had learned. I expected to research users, create personas, map user journeys, design prototypes and test solutions.

Instead, my first internship introduced me to something I had never worked with before: AI-assisted product development.

And it challenged not only how I designed, but how I understood my role as a designer.

My first day at Cway.

I got my internship at Cway, a Swedish startup that develops B2B SaaS product for the FMCG industry — companies that produce things like food, drinks and other fast-moving consumer goods.

On my first day, I received:

  • A work email
  • A Slack account
  • Access to Linear
  • Access to GitHub
  • Access to the company’s product
  • And an account for Claude

It felt less like a traditional onboarding process and more like someone had handed me the keys to a moving car while I don’t have a driving license!

Now it’s where the challenges begin.

The UX process I knew did not fit

At school, my UX projects usually followed a clear sequence:

Research → identify user needs → define problems → brainstorm → create wireframes → build a prototype → test → validate

It was structured. It was familiar. It made sense.

But startups do not always have the time, people or routines required to follow a perfect process.

Cway was a small team where everyone had several responsibilities. The CEO was also the product owner. The CTO was also a full-stack developer. The backend developer also worked with frontend. The project manager also worked with marketing.

And I was the only UX designer.

My supervisor worked mostly remotely, and there was no detailed UX handbook waiting for me. No step-by-step process. No established design team to observe.

I had to figure out how UX could fit into the way the company already worked.

For the first two weeks, I did what I knew.

I researched the company and the product. I talked to people in the office. I spoke with sales and the CEO to understand the users and the problems they encountered. I explored the product myself, documented usability issues and looked at competitors.

I created personas, user flows and problem statements.

I had gathered a lot of information.

Then I reached the point where I wanted to turn my ideas into design.

That was when everything changed.

“We don’t use Figma”

I opened Figma.

My CEO looked at me and said:

“We don’t use Figma.”

I was in shock.

I had spent a year living in Figma. I thought about components, variables and design systems constantly. Sometimes it felt like I was seeing Figma in my sleep.

And now I was being told not to use it.

What was I supposed to do?

Then came the explanation:

“We gave you the tool.”

The tool was Claude. Right. The team had been building the product with Claude from the beginning.

This was the moment when I understood that not every workplace uses the tools I had learned at school. There was no point trying to force my familiar process onto a team that had developed a completely different way of working.

If I wanted to contribute, I had to learn their language.

Learning a new design language

During the internship, I took an online masterclass to understand Claude beyond the basic chat interface.

I explored Claude for:

  • Chat
  • Design
  • Code
  • Cowork
  • Working with GitHub
  • Building directly in the codebase

At the same time, I had to learn how the team worked with staging environments, pull requests and the existing product. My vocabulary started to change.

Suddenly, I was talking about:

  • APIs
  • MCP
  • Metadata
  • Context windows
  • Tokens
  • Prompt engineering
  • Codebases
  • Work trees
  • Subagents
  • Pipelines
  • Deployment

These were the words I had never expected to use frequently as a UX student.

But they became part of my design process.

From designing screens to designing in the product

My workflow at Cway gradually changed.

It became something like this:

Research
→ Understand the product and business context
→ Define user problems
→ Form hypotheses
→ Explore design improvements
→ Build directly in the product with Claude Code
→ Experience the result in the browser
→ Identify friction
→ Refine the solution
→ Push changes to GitHub
→ Collect feedback
→ Iterate

The biggest difference was that I no longer had to stop at a static design.

Instead of only describing an idea in Figma, I could build a version of it directly into the working product. I could experience it in the browser, notice what felt wrong and adjust it.

The distance between an idea and something testable became much shorter.

This did not mean that the design process became effortless.

I still had to understand the problem. I still had to make decisions. I still had to recognise when a solution was confusing, unnecessary or simply not good enough.

Claude could help me move faster, but it could not decide what was worth building. That was still my responsibility.

I was no longer “just” a UX designer

At some point during the internship, I realised that I no longer felt like I was working only as a UX designer.

I was also becoming:

  • A product thinker
  • A prompt engineer
  • An AI tool learner
  • An interface between design and development
  • An orchestrator of tools and workflows

This was both exciting and slightly overwhelming.

When you study UX, it is easy to imagine that your role is mainly about understanding users and designing interfaces.

In reality, design is deeply connected to the product, the business, the technology and the people building it.

A good idea is not enough, you also need to understand the environment where that idea will live. You need to know how your team works. You need to communicate with developers. You need to understand constraints. You need to adapt when the process changes.

And sometimes, you need to be willing to put down the tool you know best.

What my first internship taught me

1. A process is a tool, not a law

The UX process I learned at school was useful. It gave me a foundation.

But it was not a set of rules that every workplace had to follow.

Real projects are often messier: research, design, development and testing can overlap. Sometimes you have to make progress with incomplete information.

The process needs to serve the project, not the other way around.

2. Learn the tools your team actually uses

It is easy to become attached to the tools we already know.

But professional design is not about proving that your favourite tool is the best one. It is about helping the team solve real problems.

If the team uses Claude, GitHub and a browser-based workflow, then those are the tools I need to understand.

3. AI does not replace design judgement

AI can help generate ideas, write code and accelerate experimentation.

But it does not remove the need for human judgement.

Someone still has to ask: Is this the right problem to solve? Does this help the user? Does this fit the product? Is this workflow understandable? What might go wrong?

The faster the tools become, the more important these questions become.

4. Your first internship is not supposed to feel comfortable

Starting my first internship, I wanted to feel prepared.

Instead, I often felt like I was learning everything at once.

I had to understand a new company, a new product, a new team and a new way of working. I had to learn tools that were not part of my education and make decisions without always knowing whether I was doing things “the right way.”

But maybe that is what a first internship is supposed to be. Not a place where you already know everything, but a place where you discover what you still need to learn.

Because working at a startup is challenging. There is a lot to do, the pace is high and there is often no manual telling you what to do next.

But I am starting to believe that this is also where some of the best learning happens.

Through trying.

Through making mistakes.

Through adapting.

And occasionally, through opening Figma and hearing:

“We don’t use Figma.”

medium.titulo: Where Hindsight Recall Fits in My Agent’s Request Path
medium.resumo: How TOM runs memory recall alongside parsing, and why only some handlers use what comes back
medium.conteudo_html:
How TOM runs memory recall alongside parsing, and why only some handlers use what comes back

If you add memory to an agent with several front ends, you have to decide where recall lives. Put it in each interface and you write it three times. Put it in the model prompt and you pay for it on every request, whether it matters or not.

TOM has a Tkinter desktop app, a CLI and voice input. I put Hindsight agent memory in the shared agent core, started it in parallel with parsing, and let each handler decide whether to use the result.

One core, three front doors

tom_desktop_app.py is the Tkinter UI. main.py is the CLI. Voice has a conversation mode and an action mode. They differ in how they show results, but task requests from all three end up in TomAgent.execute_task() in agent.py. Action-like voice requests are handed straight to it.

Because they share a core, they share a memory bank. A preference stored through one interface is available to the others, since the bank ID is a property of the install.

The interfaces still own what only they can do. The desktop app installs a dialog as the approval provider (approval_manager.provider = self._ask_approval), because a GUI has no console to read a yes or no from. The core asks for approval the same way everywhere; each front end decides how to ask. It also prints the memory status line into the chat at startup, for example Long-term memory: ONLINE — Hindsight Cloud, bank ‘tom-…’, so I always know whether memory is on before I rely on it.

The request path

execute_task() starts with a safety check. Then, if memory is available, it launches recall as a background task and awaits parsing, so the two overlap:

(agent.py).

Recall is time-boxed. arecall() wraps the call in a timeout slightly longer than the client’s, so a slow memory server can delay a task by a bounded amount and never hangs it.

After parsing, three routers take over:

• command_router classifies the request and attaches metadata, such as whether it needs approval.

• engine_router matches specialized engines with conservative regular expressions.

• skill_manager checks for a local skill when nothing more specific applies.

Where recalled memory actually goes

This is the part I want to be honest about. The general recall (limit=8) fills self._recalled. Handlers that draft emails or documents call _build_memory_context() and fold the hits into their prompts. Voice mode does the same with limit=5.

Most other handlers never read it. File organization does its own, narrower recall: a file-specific query, filtered to preference and correction tags, parsed into rules. I did not want a pile of recalled sentences in every prompt. Some requests benefit from memory, some are harmed by extra context, and the handler knows which.

Opting a handler in

Adding memory to a handler is one line plus a decision about the prompt:

memory_context = self._build_memory_context(command)

_build_memory_context() combines long-term recall with other context sources into a block of text. The handler then places that block in its own prompt, wherever it belongs. There is no global prompt injection to reason about, and a handler that never calls it never sees memory. Setting HINDSIGHT_ENABLED=0 switches the whole layer off, and the status line says so.

That shape is what I would reuse for any agent that sits behind several channels. A support agent answering over chat, email and phone, or an accounts-payable agent fed from a mailbox and a shared folder, needs one memory bank behind one core, not one per channel.

Before and after

Same request, “organize my downloads,” first with no stored preferences, then after one correction and a reworded request:

The first plan sent PDFs to Documents/. The second sent them to Invoices/. The card exists because I did not want memory to be invisible: if TOM used a rule, it says so.

Failure handling

Memory is optional by design. The wrapper catches missing packages, bad configuration and client errors. A failed recall returns an empty list. A failed retain goes to a local journal and a pending queue, and the queue is retried after the next successful retain or recall. With Hindsight down, TOM still organizes files. It just falls back to defaults.

What did not work as I hoped

There are two recall paths, and that duplication is a cost. A general one feeds prompts, and a specialized one feeds the file planner. They can disagree if the bank is inconsistent. I accepted that because merging them would mean either bloating prompts or losing the tag filters.

Rules from memory also apply only to handlers that consult them. Adding a new handler does not give it memory for free; you have to call recall on purpose.

Takeaways

• Put recall in the shared core. Interfaces stay thin, and memory follows the user across them.

• Overlap recall with parsing. Recall becomes a parallel step instead of a serial one.

• Let handlers opt in. Not every request wants memory in its prompt.

• Show what memory did. A visible card builds more trust than a better prompt.

• Time-box everything. A memory layer should never be the reason a task hangs.

For the mechanics of recall and retain, see the Hindsight documentation. Vectorize’s page on what agent memory is is a good primer, and the code lives in the TOM repository.

medium.titulo: I Put ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to Work on One Real Client Project
medium.resumo: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to Work on One Real Client Project
medium.conteudo_html:
ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to Work on One Real Client Project

A client recently gave me a straightforward SEO content project.

The brief was simple: create a well-researched article that was useful, optimized for search, easy to read, and natural enough that it didn’t sound machine-written.

Normally, I’d pick my usual AI tool and get started.

But this time, I had a different idea.

What if I gave the exact same project to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini?

So I ran the experiment.

I gave all three tools the same brief, the same target audience, and the same SEO requirements.

The results were surprisingly different.

The Test

I created one detailed brief containing:

  • Target keyword
  • Search intent
  • Target audience
  • Article length
  • Tone of voice
  • SEO requirements
  • Content structure
  • Key points to cover

Then I gave the same instructions to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

I wasn’t trying to find out which AI was “smarter.”

As a freelancer, I care about something much more practical:

Which tool helps me deliver better client work in less time?

ChatGPT: Fast and Flexible

ChatGPT was the first tool I tested.

It produced a complete outline and first draft quickly.

What impressed me most was how easy it was to refine.

I could ask:

“Make this sound more natural.”

“Rewrite this for a US audience.”

“Add a practical example.”

“Make the introduction more engaging.”

The response would change almost immediately.

For freelance content writers and digital marketers, that flexibility can save a lot of editing time.

I found ChatGPT particularly useful when I needed to move quickly from an idea to a workable draft.

Claude: Strong on Writing

Claude gave me a different experience.

The initial article felt more polished.

The transitions were smooth, the paragraphs were easy to follow, and the overall structure felt natural.

For a long-form article, that matters.

A business owner in London or a startup founder in Dubai doesn’t necessarily want a huge amount of information. They want clear writing that gets to the point and gives the reader something useful.

Claude performed well in that area.

The only issue was that some sections sounded slightly too formal for the conversational style I wanted.

A few additional prompts fixed that.

Gemini: Useful for Ideas and Research

Gemini stood out in another area.

It was useful when I wanted to explore different angles around the topic.

It helped me think about related questions, potential subtopics, and additional ideas that could make the article more comprehensive.

For example, if I were creating content for a Dubai-based digital marketing agency, I could use it to brainstorm questions potential business clients might have.

The first draft still needed more editing than the other two.

But as an idea-generation and research assistant, it was useful.

The Comparison

CategoryChatGPTClaudeGeminiSpeedVery FastFastFastFirst DraftStrongStrongGoodWriting FlowVery GoodExcellentGoodSEO ContentStrongStrongGoodEditingExcellentExcellentGoodIdea GenerationExcellentVery GoodExcellentBest UseDrafting & RefiningLong-Form WritingResearch & Brainstorming

The Biggest Surprise

I expected one tool to clearly beat the other two.

It didn’t.

Instead, I found that each tool was better suited to different parts of the project.

ChatGPT helped me move quickly.

Claude helped me improve the writing.

Gemini helped me explore additional ideas.

That changed the way I think about AI.

Instead of asking, “Which AI is the best?”

I now ask:

“Which AI is best for this particular task?”

That’s a much more useful question.

How I’d Use Them for Real Client Work

If I were working with a US e-commerce company, I might use ChatGPT to build the initial content structure and draft.

For a UK-based agency producing long-form thought leadership content, Claude could be useful for refining the writing and improving flow.

For a UAE startup creating market-focused content, Gemini could help brainstorm topics, questions, and different content angles.

But I wouldn’t blindly send the output from any of them to a client.

That’s where freelancers still add the most value.

I fact-check.

I edit.

I add client-specific information.

I adjust the tone.

And most importantly, I understand the audience.

AI can produce the ingredients.

The freelancer still needs to prepare the meal.

The Mistake I Almost Made

At first, I thought better prompts were the entire secret.

They’re not.

The quality of the result depends heavily on the information you provide.

Compare these two prompts:

“Write an SEO article about digital marketing.”

And:

“Write a 1,000-word article for small business owners in the UK. Explain three practical digital marketing strategies, use simple language, include real-world examples, and focus on informational search intent.”

The second prompt gives the AI something to work with.

The lesson was simple:

Better briefs produce better results.

What I Learned

This experiment changed my freelance workflow.

I no longer feel like I need to choose one AI tool and use it for everything.

Instead, I treat them as different assistants.

One helps me draft.

One helps me edit.

One helps me brainstorm.

That approach saves time without removing the human side of the work.

And that’s especially valuable when you’re working with clients across markets like the US, UK, and UAE, where expectations for quality, communication, and professionalism can be high.

The real advantage isn’t using more AI tools.

It’s knowing when to use each one.

If you’re a freelancer, agency owner, SEO specialist, or digital marketer, try the same experiment with one of your real projects.

Give the same brief to all three.

Compare the output.

Then ask the question that actually matters:

Which tool helps me deliver better work, faster?

That’s a much better AI test than simply asking which chatbot is “the best.”

medium.titulo: Why I Didn’t Pick the Most Popular Framework for My Game Site
medium.resumo: I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.
medium.conteudo_html:
I built the same MVP with Next.js 14 and Vue 3 + Vite. Three days later, I realized the framework wasn’t the real decision at all.

Before I started building my game collection site, I spent a long time agonizing over the tech stack.

Next.js 14 is the popular choice right now. App Router + SSG looks perfect for a content site. Vue 3 + Vite is known for being lightweight — smaller first-load JS, faster builds. Both have good arguments. There are plenty of comparison articles online, but reading them only made me more indecisive. They all compared specs, but none of them told me how to choose given my constraints.

So I stopped reading and started building. Same MVP, two stacks, one after the other. Let the data decide.

What I found was something more important than the stack itself.

What I Actually Cared About

Most people start tech selection by comparing feature lists. But feature lists are infinite. What actually constrains you are just a few things. I wrote down three hard constraints:

One: SEO had to work. Most traffic for a game site comes from search engines. Game detail pages must be crawlable. This wasn’t “nice to have” — it was mandatory.

Two: First load had to be fast. LCP under 2.5s on mobile 4G. Users have only a few seconds of patience. Slow means gone.

Three: The game iframe couldn’t block the main thread. While browsing the list page, no game runtime code should load. I’ll come back to this point, because it turned out to be the real key.

These three constraints ended up driving my entire decision.

Day 1: Next.js Version — Static Export Taught Me a Lesson

I built the homepage, category pages, and game runtime page with Next.js 14 App Router, using output: 'export' for pure static export, deployed to Vercel.

Homepage and category pages generated HTML correctly. But /play/[id] all returned 404.

After digging in: App Router with output: 'export' doesn’t support dynamic routes by default unless you explicitly define generateStaticParams. This is heavily discussed in the community; developers have reported that “the latest Next.js App Router doesn’t support dynamic routes with static generation.”

Worse, even after defining generateStaticParams, all game IDs have to be pre-generated at build time. If the game count grows to hundreds, every new game triggers a full rebuild, and CI time grows exponentially.

I tried @falsefoundation/next-dynamic-exports, which supports dynamic routes by generating fallback pages, but it requires web server rewrite rules, adding deployment complexity.

Then I tried a different approach: turn the game runtime page from a dynamic route into a client-rendered static shell — the /play page reads the game ID via useSearchParams after loading. This bypasses the generateStaticParams limitation, but the game runtime page is no longer prerendered, so SEO suffers. My trade-off: the game runtime page has low SEO value anyway (users arrive from the detail page), so it’s acceptable.

Next.js version data: Homepage LCP 1.2s (mobile 4G throttling), first-load JS ~85KB (gzip), build time 12s.

（When publishing to Medium, embed the code snippets above via Gist to avoid formatting issues. Same for the rest of this article.）

Day 2: Vue 3 + Vite Version — Genuinely Lightweight

Vue’s dev experience was excellent. Vite cold start under 1 second, hot updates nearly imperceptible, build time only 6 seconds — half of Next.js. First-load JS ~50KB, nearly 40% less.

But SEO became a problem.

Vue + Vite defaults to SPA. The homepage and category pages only contain <div id="app"></div> in the HTML — crawlers see no content. The solution was to install vite-plugin-seo-prerender, which prerenders the SPA into static HTML files at build time.

Configuration is simple:

// vite.config.ts
import seoPrerender from 'vite-plugin-seo-prerender'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    seoPrerender({
      routes: ['/', '/games/puzzle', '/games/sports']
    })
  ]
})

But the plugin has a limitation: it’s only suitable for generating static HTML for a small number of pages. If the game count grows to hundreds, every game detail page needs prerendering, and build time becomes uncontrollable.

Another option is Nuxt 3, Vue’s meta-framework with built-in SSG. But that introduces another framework, contradicting the “lightweight” goal.

Vue version data: Homepage LCP 1.5s (after prerendering), first-load JS ~50KB (gzip), build time 6s.

Day 3: A Counterintuitive Finding

After both versions were running, I did one thing: recorded the full timeline from homepage to clicking “Start Game” using Chrome DevTools Performance panel on both.

Something counterintuitive came up: the performance difference between the two versions was far smaller than I expected.

The Next.js version had 35KB more first-load JS, but on 4G that’s about 200ms of download time. The real time sink while browsing the list page wasn’t the framework’s JS size — it was the game iframe initialization.

In the default implementation, the iframe was initialized when the game detail page mounted. Even if the iframe src pointed to an empty placeholder page, creating the contentWindow and initializing the sandbox environment still consumed main thread time. On a Moto G Power, that single operation took about 400ms.

The correct approach is the facade pattern: render only a lightweight static placeholder (thumbnail + play button) before the iframe mounts, and inject the actual iframe only when the user clicks “Start.” This matches Lighthouse’s recommendation for deferring third-party resources.

There’s a Next.js static wiki case in the DEV community that uses the facade pattern to move a YouTube iframe from hydration-time mount to click-time load, bringing mobile TBT down from destructive levels to acceptable.

This means: the framework choice’s impact on first-load performance is far smaller than the iframe initialization strategy’s impact.

I wrote this down because it directly changed my selection criteria. Before, I was comparing “whose first-load JS is smaller.” Now I was comparing “who makes the facade pattern easier to implement.”

Final Choice: Hybrid Architecture

Based on the three-day comparison, I made these decisions:

Static content pages (homepage, category pages, detail pages) use Next.js SSG.SEO works out of the box, no extra plugins. Dynamic routes have limitations, but the game detail page ID count is manageable (only 6 games initially). If the game count grows to 200+, a Headless CMS with ISR can be introduced, but that requires a server and breaks the zero-backend constraint.

The game runtime page uses an independent client-rendered shell. The game runtime page has low SEO value and doesn’t need prerendering. Use next/dynamicwith ssr: false to lazy-load the game iframe component, facade pattern: initialize the iframe only after the user clicks “Start.”

Here’s the concrete implementation:

// components/GameLauncher.tsx
'use client'
import { useState } from 'react'
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic'

const GameIframe = dynamic(() => import('./GameIframe'), {
  ssr: false,
  loading: () => <div className="h-full bg-zinc-900 animate-pulse" />
})

export default function GameLauncher({ game }) {
  const [started, setStarted] = useState(false)

  if (!started) {
    return (
      <button
        onClick={() => setStarted(true)}
        className="relative w-full aspect-video rounded-lg overflow-hidden"
      >
        <img src={game.thumbnail} alt={game.title} className="w-full h-full object-cover" />
        <div className="absolute inset-0 flex items-center justify-center">
          <svg width="64" height="64" viewBox="0 0 64 64">
            <circle cx="32" cy="32" r="30" fill="rgba(0,0,0,0.6)" />
            <polygon points="26,20 26,44 46,32" fill="white" />
          </svg>
        </div>
      </button>
    )
  }

  return <GameIframe src={game.entry} gameId={game.id} />
}

ssr: false ensures the iframe component isn’t bundled into the HTML during server rendering, and only loads from the client after the user clicks. This matches Next.js’s official lazy-loading advice: for heavy components that don’t participate in SSR, use next/dynamic with ssr: false to reduce the initial bundle.

The Vue version wasn’t maintained. It builds faster and has a smaller bundle, but SEO needs extra plugins, and if the game count grows, the prerendering solution’s scalability is worse than Next.js’s SSG system.

Test conditions: MacBook Pro M1 build, iPhone 12 + Chrome DevTools 4G throttling, 10 runs each, median.

Note a counterintuitive result: Vue’s LCP was actually slower than Next.js after prerendering. The reason is that vite-plugin-seo-prerender still includes the full Vue runtime in the generated HTML, while Next.js SSG outputs cleaner HTML with lower hydration cost. This shows that “smaller first-load JS” doesn’t equal “faster first load.”

Trade-offs

Next.js build time is longer. 12s vs 6s. Every new game requires a rebuild. If the game count reaches 50, build time could exceed 30 seconds.

The Vue version was abandoned. It has better dev experience and a smaller bundle, but needs extra work on SEO and scalability. If your game site doesn’t need SEO — an internal tool or pure entertainment site — Vue + Vite is the better choice.

The hybrid architecture adds complexity. Static pages and the runtime page use different rendering strategies, requiring understanding of two sets of logic.

Unresolved

If the game count exceeds 100, generateStaticParams full pre-generation becomes a bottleneck, requiring ISR or a Headless CMS — but that’s no longer zero-backend.

I didn’t dig deep into Vue’s prerendering solution. vite-plugin-prerender-staticsupports multi-route generation and SEO meta tags, which might be enough if the game count is small.

Astro is another direction worth watching. A developer built a 50+ game site with Astro + vanilla JS, keeping the JS bundle under 100KB gzip and emphasizing “each game only loads the JavaScript it actually needs.” This approach is in the same spirit as the facade pattern. If you’re in the selection phase, it’s worth half a day to look into.

What This Means for You

If you’re making a similar tech decision, here’s my advice:

Define your hard constraints first, then look at frameworks. If your constraints are the same as mine (SEO + first load + iframe not blocking the main thread), the real decision point isn’t “Next.js or Vue” — it’s “how to implement the facade pattern.” The framework is just a container. Pick one whose downsides you can live with.

Don’t just look at first-load JS size. The Vue version was 35KB smaller, but its LCP after prerendering was actually slower. The relationship between size and performance is more complex than a spec sheet suggests.

Building both versions for three days is more useful than reading thirty comparison articles. The point of this article isn’t to tell you to pick Next.js. It’s to show you how to reach your own conclusion.

medium.titulo: Migrating From Vue 2 to Vue 3: A 3-Year Journey
medium.resumo: A story about a failed rewrite, a three-year migration, and the lesson that came out of it.
medium.conteudo_html:
A story about a failed rewrite, a three-year migration, and the lesson that came out of it.

Three years ago, I decided to upgrade our frontend — a large, Vue 2 and Vuex-based IoT platform — to Vue 3. I didn’t know at the time that it would take three years, involve a failed rewrite, a full UI revamp, and a side project that turned into my first published npm package. Here’s how it actually went.

The problem

I could already see it getting worse, not better — an outdated stack meant losing access to newer package support and missing out on the AI tooling being built for modern ecosystems.

Our frontend couldn’t run past Node 14. Vue 2 and Vuex were becoming obsolete, and it was taking a real hit on productivity: the dev server had gotten painfully slow, changes took a long time to reflect while developing, and new plugins had essentially stopped coming out for the stack. It was time to rebuild.

Attempt #1: starting from scratch

My first instinct was to do it the “right” way — start a brand-new project from scratch, outside working hours, as a proof of concept, with a clean architecture from day one.

It failed quickly. Every time a new change landed in the live product, I had to replicate it in the new codebase and test everything twice. I couldn’t keep up the pace, so I abandoned the idea.

The pivot: migrating in place

Instead of starting fresh, I decided to migrate the existing project directly. The one requirement I had going in was to keep the git history intact, so the changes stayed traceable and in sync with everything that came before.

Roughly what that looked like:

  • Removed the main configuration files needed to run the project, without touching the existing modules yet
  • Removed package.json entirely — every package was obsolete and incompatible with Vue 3, since the jump from Vue 2 to Vue 3 changed too much under the hood for any of them to carry over
  • Installed Pinia as the new store, added Vue Router for Vue 3, and set up TypeScript support
  • Commented out every route, then brought them back one at a time, fixing whatever broke along the way

The component library grind

This part applies no matter which component library you’re using: whatever version supports Vue 3 usually isn’t backward-compatible with how you were using the old one, so you end up touching almost every file that references it.

There wasn’t a single clean diff to apply — most usages stayed the same, and only a handful of patterns had actually changed. So I kept a running to-do list of whatever I found different and worked through the fixes incrementally, file by file, over time, alongside the regular folder restructuring and the move to TypeScript.

Three years later

The numbers, for what they’re worth: our CI build on Jenkins dropped from about 5 minutes to 2. The local dev server used to take roughly 20 seconds to spin up — now it’s close to instant. We’re finally on a supported Node LTS release instead of being stuck on Node 14. The whole thing just feels smoother to work in, day to day.

It was, in every sense, a three-year ultra marathon. But we came out the other side with a fully current set of dependencies and a codebase that’s actually pleasant to build on again.

The problem I didn’t see coming

Once the migration was done, I ran into something I hadn’t planned for: the client couldn’t tell that anything had changed, because the UI still looked exactly the same as before.

All that work, and from the outside, nothing looked different.

So that became the next project — a full UI revamp, .done in close collaboration with design, business, and the development team — going stakeholder by stakeholder until everyone signed off. We made the interface more user-friendly and better looking.

A detour: building my own npm package

Partway through, I hit a wall — I couldn’t find a Vue 3-compatible version of an image upload package we depended on. So I built one myself and published it to npm as vue-crop-upload. It was a good excuse to learn something new, and it's out there now for anyone else who runs into the same gap.

The lesson

Starting from scratch looked like the “right” way to do this on paper. It wasn’t the right way for our circumstances — we couldn’t pause feature work or run two codebases side by side while rebuilding everything from zero.

The incremental, in-place migration was slower to look impressive and far less satisfying to plan out. It was also the one that actually worked. Sometimes the best solution isn’t the best solution for your circumstances — the one that fits your team, your timeline, and your constraints usually wins.

Thanks for reading — if you’ve gone through something similar, I’d love to hear how you approached it.
